{{Short description|Smoothing of data points, digital filter}}

'''Whittaker–Henderson smoothing''' or '''Whittaker–Henderson graduation''' is a [[digital filter]] that can be applied to a set of digital data points for the purpose of [[smoothing]] the data, that is, to increase the precision of the data without distorting the signal tendency.<ref>{{citeQ|Q134457353}}</ref>

It was first introduced by [[Georg Bohlmann]]<ref>Bohlmann, G., 1899. Ein ausgleichungsproblem. Nachrichten Gesellschaft Wissenschaften Gottingen, Math.-Phys. Klasse 260–271.</ref> (for order 1). [[E. T. Whittaker|E.T. Whittaker]] independently proposed the same idea in 1923<ref>{{citeQ|Q127739868}}</ref> (for order 3).
[[Robert_Henderson_(mathematician)|Robert Henderson]] contributed to the topic by his two publications in 1924<ref>Henderson, R., 1924. A new method of graduation, Trans. Actuarial Soc. Amer. 25, 29–40.</ref> and 1925.<ref>Henderson, R., 1925. Further remarks on graduation, Trans. Actuarial Soc. Amer. 26, 52–57.</ref>
Whittaker–Henderson smoothing can be seen as P-Splines of degree 0. The special case of order 2 also goes under the name [[Hodrick–Prescott filter]].

== Mathematical formulation ==
For a signal <math>y_i</math>, <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>, of equidistant steps, e.g. a [[time series]] with constant intervals, the Whittaker–Henderson smoothing of order <math>p</math> is the solution to the following [[Regularized least squares|penalized least squares]] problem:
:<math>
\hat{x} = \operatorname{argmin}_{x_1, \ldots, x_n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i=1}^{n-p} (\Delta^p x_i)^2 \,,
</math>
with penalty parameter <math>\lambda</math> and difference operator <math>\Delta</math>:
:<math>
\begin{align}
   \Delta x_i &= x_{i+1} - x_i \\
   \Delta^2 x_i &= \Delta(\Delta x_i) = x_{i+2} - 2 x_{i+1} + x_i
\end{align}
</math>
and so on.

For <math>\lambda \rightarrow \infty</math>, the solution converges to a polynomial of degree <math>p-1</math>. For <math>\lambda \rightarrow 0</math>, the solution converges to the observations <math>y</math>.

The Whittaker-Henderson method is very similar to modern [[Smoothing spline]] methods; the latter use derivatives rather than differences of the smoothed values in the penalty term.

==Properties==
* Reversing <math>y</math> just reverses the solution <math>\hat{x}</math>.
* The first <math>p</math> moments of the data are preserved, i.e., the j-th momentum <math>\sum_i y_i^j = \sum_i \hat{x}_i^j</math> for <math>j=0\ldots p</math>.
* Polynomials of degree <math>p-1</math> are unaffected by the smoothing.

==Binomial data==
Henderson<ref>{{cite conference|last=Henderson|first=R.|date=1924|title=Some points in the general theory of graduation|book-title=Proceedings of the International Mathematical Congress held in Toronto, August 11-16, 1924|volume=2|pages=815-820|url=https://archive.org/details/proceedings-of-the-international-mathematical-congress-1924-vol-2/page/815/mode/2up}}</ref> formulates the smoothing problem for binomial data, using the logarithm of binomial probabilities in place of the error sum-of-squares,
:<math>
\log Q = \sum_x \left\{ \theta_x \log q_x + (E_x-\theta_x) \log ( 1-q_x ) \right\}
</math>
where <math>E_x</math> is the number of binary observations made at <math>x</math>; <math>q_x</math> is the probability that the event of interest is realized, and <math>\theta_x</math> is the number of instances in which the event is realized.

Henderson applies the logistic transformation to the probabilities <math>q_x</math> for the penalty term,
:<math>
\lambda_x = \log \frac{q_x}{1-q_x}; \mbox{ and }  y=\sum_x \left ( \Delta^3 \lambda_x \right )^2.
</math>
Then, Henderson places an ''a priori'' probability on a set of graduated values,
:<math>
\log P = f(y)
</math>
for a decreasing function <math>f(y)</math> (<math>f(y) = -y</math> for the usual quadratic penalty). Henderson's penalized criterion is
:<math>
\log P + \log Q,
</math>
which is a modification of the Whittaker-Henderson smoothing criterion for binomial data.
